modules.title: DevOps at Cloud-Native Parity
modules.summary: The toolchain in adoption order: the seven DevOps roles, Linux/shell/Git for DevOps, branching and PR workflows, Docker (images, layers, multi-stage builds), Jenkins pipelines as code with security gates, Kubernetes foundations, Ansible for fleet state, and observability with Prometheus/Grafana/Loki. Milestone projects per role.
objectives: Map the seven DevOps roles and their boundaries; sequence your own path.
Build Docker images with multi-stage builds; explain layers and caching.
Write Jenkins pipelines as code with artifact management and security gates.
Deploy to Kubernetes: pods, services, deployments, ConfigMaps/secrets, ingress, Helm.
Query Prometheus with PromQL; build Grafana dashboards and alerts.

notes.title: Roles, Linux, Git: the foundation
notes.body:
The **seven roles** (build, release, operate, observe, secure, automate, collaborate — boundaries vary by org) give the path its sequence. **Linux/shell/Git for DevOps**: administration fluency, scripting, and **branching strategies** (trunk-based vs GitFlow — know the trade-offs), PR review discipline, GitHub Actions basics, monorepo vs polyrepo.

- Golang/Python for tooling: glue languages for operators — CLIs, controllers, automation scripts
- Branching: trunk-based (small teams, fast) vs GitFlow (release trains, overhead) — match the strategy to the release cadence
- PR review: small diffs, automated checks first, human review for design — review latency is a DORA metric in disguise
- Actions basics: workflows, jobs, runners, secrets — CI as code, versioned with the repo

notes.title: Docker and CI/CD: build and ship
notes.body:
**Docker**: images and **layers** (each instruction a cached layer — order Dockerfile for cache hits), the Dockerfile (multi-stage builds: compile in one stage, ship a slim runtime), registries (tagging discipline: immutable tags for releases).

**CI/CD with Jenkins**: pipeline as code (Jenkinsfile), agents and stages, artifact management (immutable artifacts, SBOMs), **security scanning gates** (SAST/dependency scan in the pipeline — fail the build, not the audit).

- Multi-stage: `FROM golang:1.22 AS build` → `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static` — 800MB becomes 15MB
- Layer caching: put slow-changing instructions (deps) early, fast-changing (source) late
- Pipeline stages: lint → test → build → scan → push → deploy — gates between each, not after all

notes.title: Kubernetes, Ansible, observability: run it
notes.body:
**Kubernetes foundations**: pods, services, deployments (rolling updates), ConfigMaps/secrets, ingress, Helm basics (charts as packages).

**Ansible**: playbooks for fleet state, roles, Vault for secrets, idempotent operations (cross-link: IL-04 Module 4 is the deep dive).

**Observability**: metrics and **PromQL** (`rate(http_requests_total[5m])`), alerting (alert on symptoms, not causes), Grafana dashboards (RED/USE methods), Loki for log aggregation.

- Deployment strategy: rolling update with readiness probes — zero-downtime is a probe configuration
- ConfigMaps vs secrets: secrets are base64, not encrypted — know the actual security boundary (etcd encryption, RBAC)
- Alerting: page on user-facing symptoms (latency, error rate); ticket on causes (disk filling)
- The milestone arc: containerize → pipeline → deploy → observe — each tool proven by a running system

cards.back: Compile in a fat stage, ship a slim runtime — 800MB build env becomes a 15MB image.
Slow-changing instructions early (deps), fast-changing (source) late — maximize cache hits.
Trunk-based: small teams, fast cadence, short-lived branches. GitFlow: release trains, more ceremony.
Both inject config; secrets are base64 (not encrypted) — real boundary is etcd encryption + RBAC.
Per-second request rate over a 5-minute window — the RED method's R.
Page on symptoms (latency, errors — user-facing); ticket on causes (disk, certs).

quiz.explain: Source changes fastest — put it last so dependency layers stay cached.

choices: in the pipeline before push/deploy — fail the build
quiz.explain: Shift-left: SAST/dependency scans gate the pipeline; failing the build beats failing the audit.

quiz.q: K8s rolling update with zero downtime needs?
quiz.explain: Readiness probes gate traffic to new pods; the rolling strategy replaces gradually.
ansible-vault encrypts secrets at rest in version control — distinct from HashiCorp Vault.
Rate, Errors, Duration — the request-centric dashboard method (USE is for resources).

choices: monorepo: atomic cross-service changes, tooling cost; polyrepo: autonomy, versioning overhead
quiz.explain: Atomicity vs autonomy — match to org size and release coupling.

modules.title: Cloud-Native: The Kubernetes Certification Stack
modules.summary: KCNA → CKA → CKAD → CKS: the full Kubernetes certification ladder. Architecture and etcd, workloads and scheduling, services and networking, storage and troubleshooting (CKA); application design and deployment for developers (CKAD); cluster/system hardening, supply-chain and runtime security with Falco/seccomp/AppArmor (CKS). All performance-based — practiced in live clusters.
objectives: Explain Kubernetes architecture: API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd, kubelet.
Schedule and troubleshoot workloads: deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets, jobs.
Configure services, ingress, network policies, and persistent storage.
Harden clusters: RBAC, pod security, image supply chain, runtime policies.

notes.title: KCNA + CKA: architecture and administration
notes.body:
**KCNA**: Kubernetes architecture (control plane vs nodes), cloud-native principles (microservices, immutable infra), GitOps concepts, observability basics — the vocabulary exam.

**CKA**: **etcd** (the cluster's brain — backup/restore it), workloads and scheduling (taints/tolerations, affinity, resource requests/limits), services and networking (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer, DNS, CNI at concept level), storage (PV/PVC, StorageClasses), and **troubleshooting** (the largest hidden domain — broken clusters, fix them live).

- etcd backup: `etcdctl snapshot save` — know the flags; restore is the tested skill
- Requests vs limits: requests schedule, limits throttle/kill — set requests honestly, limits defensively
- Troubleshooting method: `kubectl describe` → `kubectl logs` → events → kubelet — the same order every time
- CKA is 2 hours, performance-based, with docs allowed — speed with kubectl (`-o yaml --dry-run=client`, aliases) is the exam skill

notes.title: CKAD: the developer's exam
notes.body:
**CKAD**: application design (multi-container pods, init containers), deployment configuration (probes, rolling updates, rollbacks), observability for developers (logs, metrics endpoints), services and networking for apps.

- Imperative speed: `kubectl run/create/expose` with `--dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml` — generate, don't hand-write
- Probes: liveness (restart me) vs readiness (don't send traffic) vs startup (slow starters) — misconfigured probes are the #1 self-inflicted outage
- ConfigMaps/secrets as env vs volumes: env for simple, volumes for files and rotation
- 2 hours, performance-based — the fastest typists with the best aliases win; it's a feature, not a bug

notes.title: CKS + KCSA: the security tier
notes.body:
**CKS** (requires CKA): cluster hardening (API server flags, etcd TLS, kubelet auth), system hardening (least-privilege OS), **supply-chain security** (image scanning, ImagePolicyWebhook, signed images with cosign), runtime security (**Falco** rules, seccomp profiles, AppArmor).

**KCSA**: cloud-native security overview and Kubernetes security fundamentals — the associate on-ramp.

- Pod Security Standards: privileged → baseline → restricted — know what each forbids
- Falco: runtime threat detection on syscalls — write a rule that alerts on unexpected shell in a container
- seccomp/AppArmor: constrain what a compromised container can *do* — defense in depth past the image
- Admission control: the policy enforcement point — where supply-chain rules actually bite

cards.back: The cluster's source of truth — all state lives here. Back it up: etcdctl snapshot save.
Requests: scheduling guarantee. Limits: throttle (CPU) or kill (memory). Set honestly/defensively.
Liveness: restart the container. Readiness: remove from service endpoints. Startup: for slow starters.
2-hour performance-based, docs allowed. Speed with kubectl is the skill.
Privileged → baseline → restricted (most locked down).
Runtime syscalls — detects anomalous behavior in running containers.

quiz.q: etcd data lost, no backup. Outcome?
quiz.explain: etcd IS the cluster state. No backup = rebuild. Back it up.
OOMKill = cgroup limit hit. Check limits against real usage (metrics-server).

choices: kubectl create deploy x --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml
quiz.explain: Imperative generation is the CKA/CKAD speed technique.

quiz.q: Image pull from untrusted registry: CKS control?
quiz.explain: Supply chain: scan, sign (cosign), enforce at admission — defense at the gate.

quiz.q: seccomp profile on a pod provides?
choices: syscall filtering — limits what a compromised container can invoke
quiz.explain: seccomp constrains the syscall surface — defense in depth past the image boundary.

choices: pod removed from service endpoints, no restart
quiz.explain: Readiness gates traffic, not lifecycle — liveness restarts.

modules.title: Zero-Trust Platform Architecture
modules.summary: NIST SP 800-207 as the blueprint: the seven tenets, the policy engine / policy administrator / policy enforcement point, control plane vs data plane, the trust algorithm; identity as the perimeter (phishing-resistant MFA, device posture, continuous authentication, privileged access); microsegmentation and the network pillar; deployment models (device agent/gateway, enclave, resource portal) and migration from perimeter security.
objectives: State the seven zero-trust tenets and map them to controls.
Design identity-first access: phishing-resistant MFA, device posture, continuous auth.
Plan microsegmentation: east-west inspection, software-defined perimeters, encrypted everything.
Choose a deployment model and sequence migration from perimeter security.

notes.title: SP 800-207: tenets and components
notes.body:
The **seven tenets**: (1) all data sources/services are resources; (2) all communication secured regardless of location; (3) per-session access grants; (4) dynamic policy (identity + device + behavior); (5) enterprise monitors all asset integrity; (6) auth is dynamic and strictly enforced; (7) maximum enterprise-collected info improves posture.

**Components**: **Policy Engine** (decides), **Policy Administrator** (executes: provisions credentials/config), **Policy Enforcement Point** (the gate). **Control plane** (decisions) vs **data plane** (traffic) — separate them.

**Trust algorithm**: the PE's logic — static rules vs dynamic behavioral scoring; know that 'algorithm' here means policy logic, not ML magic

- 'Never trust, always verify' is the slogan; per-session least-privilege grants are the mechanism
- The PEP is wherever the decision is enforced: gateway, agent, or enclave — placement follows the deployment model

notes.title: Identity as the perimeter
notes.body:
When the network perimeter dissolves, **identity becomes the boundary**: **phishing-resistant MFA** (FIDO2/WebAuthn — not SMS), **device posture** (managed, patched, encrypted, EDR-healthy), **continuous authentication** (re-verify on risk signals, not just at login), **privileged access** (just-in-time elevation, session recording, vaulted credentials).

- MFA strength ladder: FIDO2 > TOTP app > SMS (SIM-swap) > none — phishing resistance is the criterion
- Device posture as a policy input: unhealthy device = reduced access, automatically
- Privileged access workstations (PAWs) and tiering: don't administer the kingdom from a browsing laptop
- Cross-link: IL-11's identity defense modules go deeper — this is the platform-architecture lens

notes.title: Microsegmentation, models, migration
notes.body:
**Microsegmentation**: workload-to-workload policy (east-west), **software-defined perimeters** (authenticate first, connect second — the network is dark until verified), **east-west inspection**, **encrypted everything** (mTLS between services).

**Deployment models** (SP 800-207): device **agent/gateway**, **enclave** (per-resource PEPs), **resource portal** (gateway to legacy).

**Migration**: inventory → classify → pilot high-value resources → expand; **maturity steps** (CISA's model: traditional → advanced → optimal); **measuring**: policy coverage %, MFA enrollment, mean time to grant/revoke.

- Start where the crown jewels are — migrate the highest-value resources first
- Measure the migration: % of access decisions via PE/PEP, % phishing-resistant MFA, lateral-movement test results
- Zero trust is a strategy executed over years — the exam tests the models, the job tests the patience

cards.back: Policy Engine (decides), Policy Administrator (executes), Policy Enforcement Point (enforces).
Control: policy decisions. Data: the traffic itself. Separate them.
FIDO2/WebAuthn — cryptographic, origin-bound. SMS/TOTP are phishable.
Device agent/gateway, enclave (per-resource PEPs), resource portal.
East-west (workload-to-workload) — the lateral-movement surface.
Inventory and classify — then pilot on the highest-value resources.

quiz.q: Per-session access grants implement which tenet?
quiz.explain: Tenet 3: access is granted per session to least privilege — no standing trust.

quiz.q: PEP placement in the enclave model?
quiz.explain: Enclave: each resource (or group) gets its own PEP — fine-grained enforcement.
FIDO2 is origin-bound cryptography — the phishing site can't relay it.

choices: east-west = internal workload traffic; north-south = in/out of the perimeter
quiz.explain: Microsegmentation targets east-west — where lateral movement happens.
CISA's zero-trust maturity model: traditional, advanced, optimal across pillars.
SDP: the network is dark until identity+posture verify — then connectivity is granted.

modules.title: Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
modules.summary: HashiCorp Terraform through the Associate (003) exam: HCL and the core workflow (resources, providers, variables, outputs, plan/apply), state fundamentals then remote state with locking, module composition, workspaces, import and refactoring — plus IaC concepts and exam-day logistics.
objectives: Write HCL: resources, data sources, variables, outputs, locals.
Run the workflow: init → validate → plan → apply → destroy.
Manage state: remote backends, locking, import, refactoring moves.
Compose modules; use workspaces; pass the Terraform Associate exam.

notes.title: HCL and the core workflow
notes.body:
**Resources** (`resource "aws_instance" "web"`) declare desired state; **providers** talk to APIs; **data sources** read existing infra; **variables/outputs/locals** parameterize.

**Workflow**: `init` (providers/modules) → `validate` (syntax) → `plan` (the diff — READ IT) → `apply` (execute) → `destroy` (teardown). The plan is the code review of infrastructure — never auto-apply blind in production.

- `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `apply tfplan`: the saved plan is the auditable artifact
- Data sources bridge the brownfield: read the existing VPC instead of importing everything day one
- `count` vs `for_each`: for_each for named instances (stable keys); count for identical counts (fragile on removal)

notes.title: State: the crown jewels
notes.body:
**State** maps config to real resources — lose it and Terraform forgets your infrastructure. **Remote state** (S3 + DynamoDB lock, Terraform Cloud, GCS): shared, **locked** (no concurrent applies corrupting state), versioned.

**Import**: `terraform import aws_instance.web i-12345` brings brownfield under management (then write the config to match). **Refactoring**: `moved` blocks rename without destroy/recreate.

- State locking: DynamoDB (or native S3 locking now) — concurrent applies without locking corrupt state
- Never hand-edit state except via `terraform state mv/rm` — and back it up first
- Workspaces: `terraform workspace new prod` — same config, separate states (fine for small setups; separate configs for serious multi-env)

notes.title: Modules and the Associate exam
notes.body:
**Module composition**: root module calls child modules (`source = "./modules/vpc"` or registry); inputs via variables, outputs bubble up. Registry modules: vet them like dependencies.

**Terraform Associate (003) domains**: IaC concepts, Terraform basics, workflow (the largest), state, modules — plus exam-day logistics.

- Module design: thin root, composable children; outputs for everything the next module needs
- `terraform fmt` and `validate` in CI — IaC gets the same hygiene as app code
- Exam tip: the test loves 'what happens when' — drift (config ≠ real), taint/replace, lock contention. Reason from the state model, not memorization

cards.back: Read the plan like a code review. Save it (-out) for the auditable artifact. Never blind-apply in prod.
Concurrent applies corrupting the state file — DynamoDB/S3-native locks serialize runs.
for_each: named instances, stable on removal. count: fragile index shifts when one is removed.
Write matching config immediately — import only binds state; the config must describe it.
Refactor resources (rename/module-shift) without destroy/recreate.
The workflow (init/plan/apply) + state — reason from the state model.

quiz.explain: The plan is the diff review of infrastructure. Blind apply is how outages are born.

quiz.q: Two engineers apply simultaneously, no locking. Risk?
quiz.explain: Concurrent writes corrupt state — locking serializes applies.

quiz.q: Remove the middle of 3 count-indexed instances. Effect?
quiz.explain: count uses indices — removing #1 shifts #2→#1, forcing recreation. for_each avoids this.

quiz.q: Brownfield server must be managed: first step?
choices: terraform import, then write matching config
quiz.explain: Import binds state; config must then describe it — both steps, in that order.
terraform_remote_state data source (or stacked outputs) — composition over duplication.

choices: terraform apply to converge (after reviewing the plan)
quiz.explain: Apply converges real to config — but review the plan, because drift sometimes reveals manual hotfixes worth keeping.

modules.title: AWS Solutions Architecture: SAA-C03
modules.summary: The Solutions Architect Associate: resilient architectures (multi-AZ, decoupling, backup/DR), high-performing (compute/storage/database selection, caching, elasticity), secure applications (IAM, KMS, security groups/NACLs, WAF/Shield), cost-optimized (pricing models, S3 tiers, right-sizing) — plus Terraform reference stacks and exam prep.
objectives: Design multi-AZ resilient architectures with decoupled components.
Select compute/storage/database services by workload requirements.
Apply IAM, encryption, and network security to architectures.
Optimize cost: pricing models, storage tiers, and right-sizing.

notes.title: Resilient: design for failure
notes.body:
**Multi-AZ** (not just multi-instance): ALB across AZs, RDS Multi-AZ, S3's 11-9s. **Decouple**: SQS/SNS/EventBridge between tiers — a failed consumer retries instead of a failed request erroring. **Backup/DR**: RTO/RPO drive the choice (backup-restore → pilot light → warm standby → multi-site active).

- AZs are isolated failure domains — single-AZ is a hope, not a design
- Decoupling turns cascading failures into queue depth — monitor the queue, not just the app
- RTO/RPO first, then pick the DR pattern — the business numbers choose the architecture

notes.title: Performant + secure: choose and protect
notes.body:
**High-performing**: compute (EC2 vs Lambda vs Fargate vs ECS — by workload shape), storage (EBS gp3/io2, EFS, S3, instance store — by access pattern), databases (RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB — by query pattern), **caching** (CloudFront, ElastiCache — cache at every layer), **elasticity** (Auto Scaling on the right metric).

**Secure**: IAM (least privilege, roles not users for apps, permission boundaries), **KMS** (envelope encryption, CMKs), security groups (stateful) vs NACLs (stateless), WAF/Shield.

- Database choice is query-pattern choice: relational+complex joins → Aurora; key-value at scale → DynamoDB
- SGs are stateful (return traffic allowed); NACLs stateless (explicit both directions) — the classic exam trap
- Cache invalidation: TTLs + versioned keys — there are only two hard problems

notes.title: Cost-optimized + exam prep
notes.body:
**Cost**: pricing models (On-Demand vs Reserved vs Spot vs Savings Plans — by steadiness), **S3 tiers** (Standard → Intelligent-Tiering → Glacier — by access recency), right-sizing (Compute Optimizer), data transfer awareness (same-AZ free, cross-region metered).

**Terraform reference stacks**: the module's IaC patterns for each architecture — VPC, ALB+ASG, RDS, S3+CloudFront as composable modules.

**SAA-C03 prep**: scenario questions with 2 plausible answers — eliminate by constraint (cost? resilience? ops overhead?). Domain mapping: resilient (Modules: resilient), performant, secure, cost-optimized — the exam mirrors these four pillars.

cards.back: Instances in one AZ share a failure domain. Multi-AZ is the resilience unit.
Failures become queue depth, not errors — consumers retry instead of requests failing.
Security groups: stateful, instance-level. NACLs: stateless, subnet-level, explicit both directions.
Key-value at scale → DynamoDB. Complex relational joins → Aurora. Query pattern decides.
Auto-moves objects between access tiers — for unpredictable access patterns.
Spot: interruptible, cheapest — batch/fault-tolerant. Reserved/SP: steady-state commitment discount.

quiz.q: ALB in 2 AZs, instances in 1 AZ. Resilient?
choices: no — instances share one AZ's fate
quiz.explain: The ALB survives AZ loss; the instances don't. Resilience needs multi-AZ at every tier.

quiz.q: Order service calls inventory synchronously; inventory slowdowns cascade. Fix?
quiz.explain: Decouple with a queue: slowdowns become queue depth, retries replace errors.

quiz.q: NACL allows inbound 443 but app unreachable. Check?
choices: NACL outbound: stateless needs explicit return rule
quiz.explain: NACLs are stateless — allow the ephemeral return range outbound too.
Intelligent-Tiering auto-optimizes for unpredictable patterns.

choices: Savings Plan/Reserved for baseline + On-Demand/Spot for peaks
quiz.explain: Commit to the baseline (discount), flex the peaks (on-demand/spot).

quiz.q: Two plausible answers on SAA — tiebreaker?
choices: re-read constraints: cost? resilience? ops overhead? — the constraint picks
quiz.explain: SAA scenarios embed the deciding constraint — find it, the answer follows.

modules.title: AWS CloudOps: SysOps Administrator
modules.summary: The operations associate: deployment and provisioning (CloudFormation, blue/green, automation), reliability and business continuity (backups, multi-AZ, DR), security and compliance (IAM, CloudTrail, Config), networking and content delivery (VPC, CloudFront, Route 53), cost and performance optimization. The exam of the operator — every domain is a runbook.
objectives: Provision with CloudFormation and run blue/green deployments.
Design backup/DR to RTO/RPO with AWS Backup and multi-AZ patterns.
Operate securely: CloudTrail, Config, IAM Access Analyzer, GuardDuty.
Optimize: Cost Explorer, Compute Optimizer, S3 lifecycle, CloudFront caching.

notes.title: Deploy and provision: automation first
notes.body:
**CloudFormation** (declarative stacks, drift detection, StackSets for multi-account), **blue/green** (CodeDeploy: shift traffic, instant rollback), Systems Manager (Patch Manager, Run Command, Parameter Store — the operator's console).

- Blue/green: the rollback story is the feature — deploy without a rollback plan is a hope
- CloudFormation drift detection: find the console cowboys — then import or revert deliberately
- Golden AMIs via EC2 Image Builder: bake, test, distribute — immutable infrastructure starts here

notes.title: Reliability and security operations
notes.body:
**Reliability**: AWS Backup (centralized policies, cross-region copy), multi-AZ/Region patterns, Route 53 health checks + failover routing.

**Security/compliance**: **CloudTrail** (who did what — the audit log), **Config** (what changed — rules + remediation), IAM Access Analyzer (finds the over-permissive), GuardDuty (threat detection), Security Hub (the aggregate).

- CloudTrail vs Config: Trail = API activity; Config = resource state over time — the exam pairs them constantly
- Backup to RTO/RPO: cross-region copy for region failure; test restores (untested backups are rumors)
- GuardDuty findings → EventBridge → Lambda/SSM remediation — the automated response loop

notes.title: Network, cost, performance
notes.body:
**Networking/content delivery**: VPC (subnets, route tables, NAT, endpoints — VPC endpoints keep S3/DynamoDB traffic off the internet), **CloudFront** (cache behaviors, origins, signed URLs), Route 53 (routing policies: failover, latency, geoproximity).

**Cost/performance**: Cost Explorer + Budgets, Compute Optimizer (right-sizing), S3 lifecycle policies, GP3 over GP2 (cheaper + tunable), Graviton (price-performance).

- VPC endpoints: Gateway (S3/DynamoDB, free) vs Interface (PrivateLink, hourly) — know which services use which
- CloudFront signed URLs/cookies: private content through the CDN — the pattern for media
- The SysOps exam is scenario-dense: every question is a runbook decision — monitor → detect → respond

cards.back: Trail: who did what (API activity). Config: what changed (resource state + rules). Paired constantly.
Instant rollback — deploy safety is the point, not just zero downtime.
Gateway: S3/DynamoDB, free, route-table. Interface: PrivateLink services, hourly charge.
A rumor. Test restores on schedule — the RTO is only real if proven.
Findings → EventBridge → Lambda/SSM automation — detect to remediate without humans.

quiz.explain: Drift detection compares stack template to reality — finds the cowboys.
Origin Access Control + signed URLs: private bucket, CDN-delivered, authorized access.

quiz.q: S3 API calls must not traverse the internet?
quiz.explain: Gateway endpoint: free, route-table entry, traffic stays on the AWS network.
Commit to steady state — Savings Plans discount it ~30-70%.
Access Analyzer identifies unintended access — the least-privilege auditor.
Health-checked failover routing — DNS steers away from the dead region.

modules.title: AWS DevOps Professional: DOP-C02
modules.summary: The professional tier: SDLC automation (CodePipeline, canary/linear deployments, feature flags), IaC and configuration management at scale (CloudFormation nested/stacks, Systems Manager), resilient cloud solutions (multi-region active-active, chaos thinking), monitoring/logging (CloudWatch Logs Insights, X-Ray tracing), incident/event response (runbooks, automated remediation), security in pipelines (signing, scanning, least-privilege roles).
objectives: Build SDLC automation: pipelines, deployment strategies, automated rollbacks.
Manage IaC at scale: nested stacks, StackSets, drift governance.
Design multi-region resilience with data replication realities.
Trace and respond: X-Ray, Logs Insights, EventBridge-driven remediation.

notes.title: SDLC automation and IaC at scale
notes.body:
**SDLC**: CodePipeline (source → build → deploy stages), **deployment strategies** (canary: 10%→50%→100%; linear: 10% every N min; all-at-once: fastest, riskiest), **feature flags** (decouple deploy from release — the safest deployment is the one you can turn off).

**IaC at scale**: nested stacks (composition), **StackSets** (multi-account/region — the landing-zone tool), drift governance, Systems Manager for fleet configuration.

- Canary metrics: error rate + latency on the canary vs baseline — automatic rollback on regression
- Feature flags > deployment strategies for risk: flags turn off features without redeploying
- StackSets: one template, N accounts/regions — the org-scale deployment primitive

notes.title: Resilience and observability
notes.body:
**Resilient solutions**: multi-region active-active (Route 53 + replicated data), **chaos thinking** (Fault Injection Simulator — prove resilience, don't assume it), backup/restore vs pilot light vs warm standby vs multi-site.

**Monitoring/logging**: CloudWatch (metrics, alarms, composite alarms), **Logs Insights** (query the logs — `fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/`), **X-Ray** (distributed tracing — find the slow microservice).

- Active-active needs data replication that supports it (DynamoDB global tables, Aurora global) — compute is the easy part
- Composite alarms: reduce noise — alarm on the AND of symptoms, not each symptom
- X-Ray service map: the architecture diagram that draws itself — start every latency hunt there

notes.title: Incident response and pipeline security
notes.body:
**Incident/event response**: runbooks (SSM Automation documents), EventBridge → Lambda/SSM remediation, post-incident reviews (blameless — fix the system).

**Security in pipelines**: artifact **signing** (signer Lambda/CodeSigner — deploy only signed artifacts), scanning gates (SAST/dependency/container), least-privilege **pipeline roles** (the pipeline's IAM role is a blast radius — scope it).

- SSM Automation runbooks: the executable runbook — incident response as code
- Sign artifacts: the pipeline proves provenance — unsigned artifacts don't deploy
- DOP-C02 is the longest exam (180 min): pace for scenarios, eliminate by constraint, flag the 50/50s

cards.back: Canary: % steps with metric gates. Linear: fixed % per interval. All-at-once: fastest, no safety.
Risk: turn off the feature without redeploying — decouple deploy from release.
One template across N accounts/regions — org-scale IaC.
Distributed tracing — the service map that draws itself; start latency hunts there.
Least privilege — the pipeline role is a blast radius; scope it to exactly the deploy actions.
180 minutes of scenarios — eliminate by constraint, flag 50/50s, keep moving.

quiz.q: Deploy to 1000 instances, catch regressions early?
quiz.explain: Canary + automatic rollback on error/latency regression — safety at scale.

quiz.q: Kill a bad feature without redeploying?
quiz.explain: Flags decouple release from deploy — the fastest mitigation path.
StackSets deploy templates across accounts/regions centrally.

quiz.q: Find the slow microservice in 40 services?
quiz.explain: Distributed tracing shows the latency waterfall — evidence over guessing.
FIS injects real failures — resilience is proven, not asserted.

quiz.q: Unsigned artifact reaches deploy stage. Policy?
quiz.explain: Provenance gates: only signed artifacts deploy — supply-chain discipline.

modules.title: AWS Security Specialty: SCS-C03
modules.summary: Threat detection and incident response (GuardDuty, Detective, Security Hub, Macie), security logging and monitoring (CloudTrail org trails, Config aggregators, Athena queries), infrastructure security (WAF, Shield, network firewalls, PrivateLink), IAM (permission boundaries, SCPs, ABAC, cross-account roles), data protection (KMS, envelope encryption, Macie), and the hardened landing zone (Control Tower, SCPs, detective+preventive guardrails) — plus exam prep.
objectives: Detect and respond: GuardDuty → Detective → automated containment.
Log everything: org CloudTrail, Config aggregation, Athena analysis.
Lock IAM: boundaries, SCPs, ABAC, cross-account patterns.
Protect data: KMS envelope encryption, S3 protections, Macie.
Build the hardened landing zone with preventive + detective guardrails.

notes.title: Detect, log, respond
notes.body:
**Threat detection**: GuardDuty (threat intel on logs), **Detective** (investigation graphs — pivot from finding to root cause), Security Hub (aggregated posture), **Macie** (PII in S3).

**Logging/monitoring**: **org CloudTrail** (all accounts, immutable bucket + Object Lock), **Config aggregators** (multi-account state), **Athena** (SQL over the logs — `SELECT * FROM cloudtrail WHERE eventname='ConsoleLogin'` for forensics).

**Incident response**: isolate (revoke creds, quarantine SG), eradicate, recover — with runbooks, not improvisation.

- Detective's graph: finding → entity → timeline — investigation in clicks, not grep marathons
- Org trail + Object Lock: the audit log attackers can't delete — non-negotiable
- Athena over CloudTrail: forensics without a SIEM budget

notes.title: IAM and infrastructure security
notes.body:
**IAM depth**: **permission boundaries** (max permissions for delegated admins), **SCPs** (org-level guardrails — even root can't bypass), **ABAC** (attributes in policies: `aws:PrincipalTag/team`), cross-account **roles** (no long-lived creds).

**Infrastructure**: WAF (managed rules + rate limiting), Shield Advanced (DDoS), Network Firewall, **PrivateLink** (service access without internet).

- SCPs don't grant — they bound. An SCP can't give what IAM doesn't allow; it can only restrict
- ABAC scales where RBAC explodes: tag the principals, tag the resources, write one policy
- Cross-account roles > access keys: temporary credentials, no rotation burden

notes.title: Data protection and the landing zone
notes.body:
**Data**: **KMS** envelope encryption (DEK per object, KEK in KMS), S3 (Block Public Access — account level, Object Lock for immutability, access points), Macie for discovery.

**Hardened landing zone**: Control Tower (account factory + guardrails), preventive (SCPs: deny unencrypted S3, deny wrong regions) + detective (Config rules, Security Hub).

- Envelope encryption: data key encrypts data, master key encrypts data key — scale without KMS throttling
- S3 Block Public Access at the ACCOUNT level — bucket policies are then defense in depth
- Landing zone = the exam's favorite scenario: new org, secure by default, compliant by construction

cards.back: IAM grants; SCP bounds (even root). SCPs restrict, never grant.
Attribute-based: one policy scales via tags — no role explosion.
Immutable multi-account audit log — attackers can't cover tracks.
DEK encrypts data; KEK (KMS) encrypts DEK — performance + centralized key control.
Account level first — then bucket policies as defense in depth.
Investigation graphs — pivot from GuardDuty finding to root cause visually.

quiz.q: Delegate admin creation but cap their power?
quiz.explain: Boundaries set the max — delegated admins can't exceed them.

quiz.q: Block all S3 public access org-wide, even for admins?
quiz.explain: SCP (preventive, org-wide, bypasses nothing) + account-level Block Public Access.

quiz.q: Forensics on 6 months of API calls, no SIEM?
choices: Athena over the org CloudTrail lake
quiz.explain: Athena SQL over CloudTrail logs — forensics without SIEM spend.
Macie scans and classifies PII at scale — the data-discovery service.
Roles: temporary credentials, no long-lived keys, no rotation burden.
Rate rules throttle request floods — pair with managed rules for OWASP patterns.

modules.title: Azure Administration: The AZ-104 Spine
modules.summary: Run Azure like a production tenant: Entra ID and RBAC (users, groups, devices, licenses; roles, scopes, least privilege, PIM), governance (management groups, subscriptions, policy, locks), storage accounts and lifecycle, compute (VMs, VMSS, containers), virtual networking, and monitoring/backup/recovery — distilled from the AZ-104 study guide into labs on a real subscription.
objectives: Administer Entra ID: users, groups, devices, licenses, PIM.
Apply RBAC: built-in/custom roles, scopes, least privilege.
Govern: management groups, policy, locks, tags.
Run storage, compute, networking, and Monitor/backup/recovery.

notes.title: Entra ID, RBAC, governance
notes.body:
**Entra ID**: users, groups (security vs M365), devices (join/register), licenses. **RBAC**: roles (Owner/Contributor/Reader + granular), **scopes** (management group → subscription → RG → resource), **least privilege**, **PIM** (just-in-time elevation — eligible, not permanent).

**Governance**: **management groups** (hierarchy for policy/RBAC), **Azure Policy** (deny/audit/deployIfNotExists — compliance as code), **locks** (CanNotDelete/ReadOnly), tagging strategy.

- PIM: eligible assignments + approval + time-bound — standing admin is the vulnerability
- Policy: assign at the management group, inherit everywhere — govern once
- Locks: CanNotDelete on production RGs — the cheapest outage insurance
- Exam weight: identity is the control plane — 20-25% of AZ-104

notes.title: Storage and compute
notes.body:
**Storage accounts**: tiers (Hot/Cool/Cold/Archive), redundancy (LRS/ZRS/GRS/RA-GRS — the durability/cost ladder), **lifecycle management** (tier down aging blobs automatically), SAS vs keys.

**Compute**: VMs (sizes, availability sets vs **zones** vs VMSS), **VMSS** (autoscale sets), containers (ACI quick, AKS serious).

- ZRS: synchronous 3-zone copy — the resilience default for regional workloads
- Lifecycle rules: Hot→Cool→Archive on age — storage cost is a policy, not a hope
- Availability zones > sets: zones survive datacenter loss; sets only rack loss

notes.title: Networking, monitor, backup
notes.body:
**Virtual networking**: VNets, subnets, **NSGs** (stateful-ish rules, default denies), peering (transit via hub), VPN/ExpressRoute, Private Endpoints (PaaS off the internet), load balancers (L4) vs Application Gateway (L7/WAF).

**Monitor**: Azure Monitor (metrics/logs), Log Analytics (KQL queries), alerts (action groups). **Backup/recovery**: Recovery Services vaults, Azure Backup policies, Site Recovery for DR.

- NSG rule order: lowest number wins — and default rules deny inbound internet
- Private Endpoints: the PaaS services join your VNet — no public endpoints
- KQL: `AzureMetrics | where MetricName == 'Percentage CPU'` — learn 5 queries, reuse forever
- AZ-104 prep: the portal is the exam — lab every objective on a real subscription

cards.back: Just-in-time elevation: eligible assignments, approval, time-bound — no standing admin.
RBAC: who can do what (access). Policy: what configurations are allowed (governance).
LRS: 3 copies, 1 datacenter. ZRS: 3 zones. GRS: + paired region. Durability/cost ladder.
Lowest rule number wins; defaults deny inbound internet, allow VNet.
PaaS services (Storage, SQL) get VNet-private IPs — off the public internet.
Identity (Entra ID/RBAC/governance) — the control plane, 20-25%.

quiz.q: Standing Global Admin for 50 admins. Fix?
quiz.explain: Eliminate standing privilege — PIM makes admin just-in-time and audited.
Policy governs configuration compliance; RBAC governs access. Different jobs.
Zones span datacenters; sets only span racks.

quiz.q: Blob untouched 180 days, rarely read. Tier?
quiz.explain: Lifecycle policy tiers it down automatically — cost follows access pattern.

choices: AGW: L7 (WAF, path routing); LB: L4
quiz.explain: Layer 7 needs (host/path routing, WAF) → App Gateway; pure L4 → LB.

choices: AzureMetrics | where MetricName has 'CPU' | summarize avg() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
quiz.explain: KQL over Log Analytics — five learned queries cover 90% of ops.

modules.title: Azure Solutions Architecture: AZ-305
modules.summary: Design, not administer: identity/governance/monitoring design, data storage design (SQL vs Cosmos DB vs Storage by pattern), business continuity (backup vs Site Recovery, RTO/RPO), infrastructure design (compute, network, migrations) — capped by the architecture capstone: a full design with trade-off documentation.
objectives: Design identity/governance for a multi-subscription enterprise.
Choose data services by workload pattern: relational, NoSQL, analytical.
Design business continuity to RTO/RPO with Site Recovery and backup.
Produce a full architecture with documented trade-offs (the capstone).

notes.title: Design identity, governance, monitoring
notes.body:
**Identity design**: Entra ID tenants, B2B/B2C shapes, hybrid (Connect sync vs federation), PIM + Access Reviews for governance.

**Governance design**: management-group hierarchy (platform/landing zones), policy initiatives, tagging + cost management, locks on the platform.

**Monitoring design**: Log Analytics workspace strategy (central vs regional), alert routing, workbooks for the business view.

- Landing zones: the enterprise scaffold — platform subscriptions + workload subscriptions, governed centrally
- Access Reviews: recurring certification of access — governance that doesn't rot
- Design answers cite the constraint: compliance? cost? operability? — the exam grades the fit

notes.title: Design data and continuity
notes.body:
**Data design**: Azure SQL (relational, familiar), **Cosmos DB** (global NoSQL, five consistency levels — pick by need), Storage (blobs/files/queues/tables by pattern), Synapse/Fabric for analytics.

**Business continuity**: **backup** (Recovery Services vaults, policies) vs **Site Recovery** (replication + failover runbooks); RTO/RPO choose the tool.

- Cosmos DB consistency: Strong → Bounded Staleness → Session → Consistent Prefix → Eventual — latency/availability trade per level
- Hot/warm/cold path: Stream (Event Hubs) → serve (Cosmos) → analyze (Synapse) — the lambda/kappa shapes
- RPO ~0 needs replication (Site Recovery/geo-replication); RPO hours tolerates backup — the numbers choose

notes.title: Design infrastructure + capstone
notes.body:
**Infrastructure design**: compute (App Service vs AKS vs VMs vs Functions — by workload), network (hub-spoke, Private Endpoints, ExpressRoute vs VPN), migrations (Azure Migrate: assess → replicate → cutover).

**Capstone**: a full design — requirements, constraints, service selections with rationale, network topology, identity plan, BC plan, cost estimate, and the trade-off log.

- Hub-spoke: shared services in the hub (firewall, DNS, VPN), workloads in spokes — peering, no transitive routing by default
- Migrate in waves: assess (Migrate appliance), replicate, test cutover, cutover — never big-bang
- The capstone is graded on rationale, not choices — two good architects can disagree; both must defend

cards.back: Enterprise scaffold: platform + workload subscriptions under management groups, governed centrally.
Strong → Bounded Staleness → Session → Consistent Prefix → Eventual. Latency/availability trade.
Peering is non-transitive by default — hub firewall/route tables enable spoke-to-spoke.
Backup: RPO-hours, cheap. Site Recovery: replication, RPO-minutes, for tier-1 workloads.
Assess → replicate → test cutover → cutover. Never big-bang.
Rationale fit to constraints — defend the trade-offs, not just the choices.

quiz.q: Global app, 10ms reads worldwide, tunable consistency?
quiz.explain: Cosmos DB: global distribution + five consistency levels — Session is the sweet spot.

choices: peering non-transitive — route via hub firewall
quiz.explain: Spoke peerings don't transit — hub NVA/firewall with UDRs enables it.
15-min RPO needs replication, not backup schedules.

quiz.q: Regulated: prove access was reviewed quarterly?
quiz.explain: Access Reviews: recurring, auditable certification campaigns.
Migrate replicates as-is — rehost now, modernize in waves after.
L7 features (WAF, path/host routing) = Application Gateway.

modules.title: Azure Network Engineering: AZ-700
modules.summary: The network specialist: core networking infrastructure (VNets, subnets, NSGs, peering, private DNS), connectivity services (VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Virtual WAN), application delivery (Load Balancer, Application Gateway, Front Door, Traffic Manager), private access to PaaS (Private Link/Endpoints, service endpoints), and secure connectivity (Azure Firewall, DDoS, Bastion) — plus exam prep.
objectives: Design VNet topology: addressing, peering, private DNS, NSGs.
Connect: VPN/ExpressRoute/Virtual WAN with the right SKU per need.
Deliver apps: Front Door vs App Gateway vs LB vs Traffic Manager.
Secure: Firewall, DDoS Protection, Bastion, Private Link.

notes.title: Core infrastructure and connectivity
notes.body:
**Core**: VNets/subnets (address space planning — no overlaps with on-prem), **NSGs** + ASGs, **peering** (transit via hub), **Private DNS zones** (VNet-linked resolution).

**Connectivity**: **VPN Gateway** (S2S/IPsec, P2S, VNet-to-VNet), **ExpressRoute** (private dedicated circuit — consistent latency, not internet), **Virtual WAN** (managed hub-and-spoke at global scale).

- Address planning is forever — overlapping CIDRs with on-prem breaks peering/VPN permanently
- ExpressRoute vs VPN: consistent private throughput vs internet-variable — the SLA decides, not the price
- Virtual WAN: Microsoft-managed hubs — global transit without building your own hub mesh

notes.title: Application delivery and private access
notes.body:
**Delivery**: Load Balancer (L4 regional), **Application Gateway** (L7 + WAF), **Front Door** (global L7 with edge PoPs), **Traffic Manager** (DNS-based global routing).

**Private access**: **Private Link/Endpoints** (PaaS into the VNet), **service endpoints** (VNet identity to PaaS, simpler but less private).

- Front Door vs App Gateway: global edge + instant failover → Front Door; regional L7 → App Gateway
- Traffic Manager: DNS-level — failover in TTL time, not instant; know the trade
- Private Link > service endpoints for data exfiltration control — endpoints keep PaaS public-adjacent

notes.title: Secure connectivity + prep
notes.body:
**Secure**: **Azure Firewall** (L3-L7, FQDN filtering, threat intel), **DDoS Protection** (network tier), **Bastion** (RDP/SSH without public IPs — no jumpbox to patch).

**AZ-700 prep**: design scenarios — pick the service by constraint (global? private? L7?). The exam tests *selection*, not syntax.

- Firewall FQDN rules: allow *.update.microsoft.com, deny the rest — egress control that actually works
- Bastion: browser-based RDP/SSH — removes the most-attacked box in the estate
- DDoS Protection: enable on the VNet housing public IPs — the attack you can't afford to learn about live

cards.back: Front Door: global edge, instant failover. App Gateway: regional L7 + WAF.
DNS — failover takes TTL time. Not instant like Front Door.
Private Link: PaaS gets VNet-private IP (stronger). Service endpoint: VNet identity, PaaS still public.
Private, consistent-latency circuit — not internet VPN variability.
Internet-facing jumpboxes — browser RDP/SSH, no public IPs to patch.
Fatal for peering/VPN — plan non-overlapping CIDRs up front, forever.

quiz.q: Global web app, instant regional failover, WAF?
quiz.explain: Front Door: global edge + instant failover + WAF — the global L7 answer.
Private Endpoint puts SQL on a VNet-private IP — off the public internet.

quiz.q: Spoke VNets need shared firewall + VPN?
quiz.explain: Hub-spoke: shared services in hub, gateway transit enabled.

quiz.q: Egress: allow only Microsoft update FQDNs?
quiz.explain: Firewall does L7 FQDN filtering — NSGs can't filter by domain.
ExpressRoute: private dedicated throughput with SLA.

choices: Private DNS zones linked to VNets
quiz.explain: Private DNS zones: VNet-linked, split-horizon resolution.

modules.title: OpenShift: Administration & Cloud-Native Development
modules.summary: Red Hat OpenShift both ways: administration (containers/Kubernetes foundations, cluster admin, storage and day-2 operations, automation and multi-cluster management — EX280/EX380) and development (containerizing apps, OpenShift deploy patterns, resilient microservices, Quarkus cloud-native development, twelve-factor capstone — EX188/EX288).
objectives: Administer OpenShift: projects, quotas, storage, day-2 operations.
Deploy with OpenShift patterns: DeploymentConfigs/routes, S2I, GitOps.
Build resilient microservices: health, config, fault tolerance.
Apply twelve-factor principles in a Quarkus capstone.

notes.title: Foundations and cluster administration
notes.body:
**Containers/K8s foundations**: images, registries, pods — OpenShift adds **projects** (namespaced multitenancy), **routes** (built-in ingress), **S2I** (source-to-image builds), **Operators** (cluster extensions as code).

**Admin core**: installation shapes (IPI/UPI), node roles, **quotas/limit ranges** (noisy-neighbor control), **storage** (OCS/ODF, StorageClasses), **day-2**: upgrades, etcd backup, cert rotation, monitoring stack.

- Projects vs namespaces: projects add the membership/annotations layer — the admin boundary
- S2I: git push → image → deploy — the developer on-ramp without Dockerfiles
- Day-2 is the job: installs are day 1; upgrades, backups, and cert rotation are the career

notes.title: Development: containerize and deploy
notes.body:
**Containerizing**: layered images, non-root users, small bases. **Deploy patterns**: Deployments/StatefulSets, routes with TLS edge/reencrypt/passthrough, **health probes**, config via ConfigMaps/secrets.

**Resilient microservices**: retries with backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads — via Service Mesh (Istio) or libraries. **Quarkus**: supersonic subatomic Java — fast startup, low memory, native via GraalVM for serverless.

- Non-root + read-only filesystem: the container security baseline
- Route TLS modes: edge (terminate at router), passthrough (to pod), reencrypt (both) — pick by compliance
- Quarkus dev mode: live reload — the inner loop that makes Java cloud-credible

notes.title: Twelve-factor capstone + exam prep
notes.body:
**Twelve-factor**: codebase, dependencies, config (env, not code), backing services (attached resources), build/release/run, stateless processes, port binding, concurrency, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs (event streams), admin processes.

**Capstone**: a twelve-factor microservice on OpenShift — S2I or Dockerfile build, route, probes, config externalized, logs to stdout, scaled horizontally.

**EX280/EX380/EX188/EX288 prep**: performance exams — tasks on live clusters. Admin: fix the broken cluster. Dev: containerize and deploy the app. Speed with `oc` is the skill.

cards.back: Project = namespace + membership/annotations — the multitenancy admin boundary.
Source-to-Image: git → image → deploy without writing Dockerfiles.
Edge (router terminates), passthrough (pod terminates), reencrypt (both).
Config in the environment, never in code — same image, all environments.
Fast startup + low memory (+ native via GraalVM) — Java for serverless/scale-to-zero.
Upgrades, etcd backup, cert rotation, monitoring — the actual job after install.

quiz.q: Dev pushes code, no Dockerfile, wants it running?
quiz.explain: S2I: source → image → deploy — the no-Dockerfile on-ramp.

quiz.q: Compliance: TLS must terminate at the pod?
quiz.explain: Passthrough: router doesn't decrypt — TLS ends at the pod.

quiz.q: Same image in dev/stage/prod differs by DB URL. Twelve-factor?
choices: config file per env in image
quiz.explain: Config in environment — one immutable image, all environments.

quiz.q: Noisy neighbor eats cluster CPU. Admin fix?
quiz.explain: Quotas bound consumption; limit ranges default it — multitenancy hygiene.
Non-root, read-only filesystem — the container security baseline.

quiz.q: Cert rotation overdue on cluster. This is?
quiz.explain: Day-2: the ongoing operational reality — upgrades, backups, rotation.

modules.title: Vault & Consul: Secrets and Service Networking
modules.summary: HashiCorp Vault (secrets engines: KV, dynamic database/AWS creds, PKI, transit; auth methods: userpass/LDAP/OIDC/Kubernetes/AWS; policies; operations: unseal, raft, DR replication) and Consul (service discovery: catalog, DNS/HTTP, health checks; service mesh: Connect, intentions, gateways) — through the Vault Associate and Consul Associate exams.
objectives: Run Vault: engines, auth, policies, unseal/raft operations.
Issue dynamic secrets and manage PKI/transit engines.
Discover services with Consul: catalog, DNS, health checks.
Mesh services: Connect intentions, gateways, mTLS.

notes.title: Vault: engines and auth
notes.body:
**Secrets engines**: **KV v2** (versioned static secrets), **dynamic** (database creds, AWS STS — leased, auto-revoked), **PKI** (internal CA — short-lived certs), **transit** (encryption-as-a-service — data never leaves your app).

**Auth methods**: userpass/LDAP (humans), **OIDC** (SSO), **Kubernetes** (pod service accounts), **AWS** (IAM-based) — machines authenticate as themselves.

**Policies**: HCL paths with capabilities (`read`, `list`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `sudo`) — least privilege for secrets.

- Dynamic secrets: credentials that expire — the leaked-credential problem solved structurally
- Transit engine: Vault encrypts/decrypts without storing data — crypto without key-management pain
- Policies are deny-by-default — nothing is readable until a policy allows it

notes.title: Vault operations reality
notes.body:
**Unseal**: Shamir keys or **auto-unseal** (KMS) — plan this before production. **Raft** integrated storage (no Consul needed anymore). **DR replication** (disaster recovery clusters), **performance replication** (read scaling).

- Auto-unseal via cloud KMS: operators never handle key shards — the sane default
- Raft snapshots: `vault operator raft snapshot save` — back up the encrypted store
- Seal migration and rekey: practice in staging — unseal ceremonies fail at 3 AM otherwise
- Monitoring: seal status, leader changes, token expiry storms — Vault is critical path, watch it like one

notes.title: Consul: discovery to mesh
notes.body:
**Service discovery**: **catalog** (registered services), **DNS** (`web.service.consul`) and **HTTP** APIs, **health checks** (only healthy instances get traffic).

**Service mesh (Connect)**: **mTLS** between services (automatic, rotated), **intentions** (allow/deny service-to-service — microsegmentation for east-west), **gateways** (mesh/ingress/terminating).

**Associate exams**: Vault Associate (engines, auth, policies, tokens/leases) and Consul Associate (discovery, mesh concepts) — concept + CLI, hands-on flavored.

- Intentions: `consul intention create -allow web api` — the firewall rule for services
- Health checks gate discovery — unhealthy never receives traffic, no LB config needed
- KV in Consul vs Vault: Consul KV is config (not encrypted by default) — secrets go in Vault

cards.back: Leaked credentials — short-lived, auto-revoked, per-request. No long-lived passwords.
Encryption-as-a-service: Vault encrypts/decrypts; your data never lands in Vault.
Deny — nothing readable until a policy explicitly allows.
web.service.consul — DNS interface to the service catalog.
Allow/deny rules for service-to-service traffic — microsegmentation for the mesh.

cards.front: Consul KV vs Vault for secrets?
cards.back: Consul KV is config (plaintext default) — secrets belong in Vault.

quiz.q: App needs DB creds, rotation required, no restarts?
quiz.explain: Dynamic: leased, auto-rotated, revoked on lease end — rotation without restarts.

modules.title: Cloud-Native Associate Stack
modules.summary: The associate tier around Kubernetes: KCNA (Kubernetes and cloud-native fundamentals), KCSA (cloud-native security associate), PCA (Prometheus observability), CCA (Cilium and eBPF networking), CAPA (Argo GitOps) — plus the consolidated associate-exam prep. The breadth layer that makes the professional exams make sense.
objectives: Pass KCNA: architecture, workloads, cloud-native principles, GitOps, observability.
Pass KCSA: cloud-native security fundamentals and the exam's domain map.
Monitor with Prometheus (PCA): metrics, PromQL, alerting.
Network with Cilium/eBPF (CCA) and deliver with Argo GitOps (CAPA).

notes.title: KCNA + KCSA: the bookends
notes.body:
**KCNA**: Kubernetes architecture, container orchestration concepts, cloud-native principles (microservices, immutable infra, declarative APIs), GitOps concepts, observability basics — the vocabulary foundation.

**KCSA**: cloud-native security overview, Kubernetes security fundamentals (RBAC, pod security, secrets, network policy), supply-chain basics — the associate security lens before CKS.

- KCNA is the on-ramp: take it before CKA if Kubernetes is new — the vocabulary pays back immediately
- KCSA domains mirror CKS at associate depth — the prep ladder is KCSA → CKS
- Both are proctored online multiple-choice — the format contrast with the performance-based CKA/CKAD/CKS

notes.title: PCA + CCA: observe and network
notes.body:
**PCA (Prometheus)**: metrics types (counter/gauge/histogram/summary), **PromQL** (selectors, rate(), aggregation), alerting rules, service discovery, the operator pattern.

**CCA (Cilium)**: **eBPF** (kernel-programmable networking — no kube-proxy iptables), Hubble (observability), network policies at L3-L7, service mesh without sidecars.

- rate() over counters, never over gauges — the PromQL trap that fails everyone once
- eBPF: programs run in the kernel safely — Cilium replaces kube-proxy with eBPF maps
- Cilium network policy enforces at L7 (HTTP methods/paths) — beyond Calico's L3/L4

notes.title: CAPA: GitOps with Argo + prep
notes.body:
**CAPA (Argo)**: GitOps principles (declared desired state in git; agents converge the cluster), **Argo CD** (sync, drift detection, automated sync policies), **Rollouts** (canary/blue-green as CRDs), projects and RBAC.

**Associate prep**: the exams are multiple-choice proctored — study the domain maps, drill the vocabulary, lab the concepts lightly (the performance depth comes at CKA/CKAD/CKS).

- GitOps: git is the source of truth; the cluster is a cache — drift is detected, not debated
- Argo CD sync waves/hooks order complex deploys — CRDs before the apps that need them
- Strategy: KCNA → (PCA or CCA by interest) → CAPA → KCSA — breadth first, then the professional tier

cards.back: Desired state declared in git; agents converge the cluster — git is truth, cluster is cache.
Counters — never gauges. The PromQL trap.
Safe kernel programs — Cilium does networking/observability without kube-proxy iptables.
Cilium: L3-L7 (HTTP-aware). Calico: L3/L4. eBPF vs iptables dataplane.
Progressive delivery (canary/blue-green) as Kubernetes CRDs.
Proctored multiple-choice — vocabulary + concepts; performance depth is the CKA/CKAD/CKS tier.

quiz.explain: rate() over a _total counter with a window — the canonical query.

scriptLabs.title: K8s: Zero-Downtime Deployment Manifests
scriptLabs.brief: Write a Deployment + Service + Ingress for a web app with readiness/liveness probes, resource requests/limits, and a rolling-update strategy. Required fragments force production hygiene.
scriptLabs.starter:
# TODO: Deployment (3 replicas, rollingUpdate), container probes (readiness /health, liveness /health),
# resources.requests/limits, Service ClusterIP, Ingress with host rule.
# Prove it: kubectl apply, then kubectl rollout status; break the image tag and watch the rollback.
scriptLabs.hint: strategy: type: RollingUpdate, maxUnavailable: 0. Probes: httpGet path /health port 8080. Resources: requests cpu 100m/memory 128Mi, limits cpu 500m/memory 512Mi.
scriptLabs.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: registry.example.com/web:1.4.2
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
          periodSeconds: 15
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
          limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  rules:
  - host: web.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /, pathType: Prefix
        backend: { service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } } }
# prove: kubectl rollout status deploy/web; then set image to :broken, watch it halt; kubectl rollout undo deploy/web

scriptLabs.brief: Write a playbook that patches a web fleet in canary waves: 1 canary host, verify, then the rest — with a handler restarting the app only on kernel change. Idempotent, with --check first.
scriptLabs.starter:

- name: patch fleet
  hosts: web
  become: true
  serial: 1  # canary wave
  tasks:
    # TODO: dnf upgrade (security), notify handler on change, wait_for port 80 after handler
  handlers:
    # TODO: restart app
scriptLabs.hint: serial: 1 for the canary (use --limit canary first), then serial: '25%' for the fleet. dnf: name='*' state=latest security=true. wait_for port 80 delay 10.
scriptLabs.solution:
---
- name: patch canary
  hosts: web-canary
  become: true
  serial: 1
  tasks:
    - name: security updates
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: '*'
        state: latest
        security: true
      notify: restart app
    - name: verify serving
      ansible.builtin.wait_for:
        port: 80
        delay: 10
        timeout: 120
  handlers:
    - name: restart app
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: app
        state: restarted
# fleet wave after canary is green:
- name: patch fleet
  hosts: web-fleet
  become: true
  serial: '25%'
  tasks:
    - name: security updates
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: '*'
        state: latest
        security: true
      notify: restart app
  handlers:
    - name: restart app
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: app
        state: restarted

scenarios.title: Region Degradation at 2 AM
scenarios.context: us-east-1 degraded: your ALB targets are unhealthy in 1 of 3 AZs. PagerDuty fires.

options.text: Check target health + AZ status; drain the bad AZ if the app is multi-AZ healthy
options.why: Scope first: one AZ degraded with healthy others = drain and ride it out, then investigate.

options.text: Fail over to another region immediately
options.why: Regional failover for an AZ issue is over-escalation — it risks the failover itself.
Restarts destroy evidence and don't fix AZ-level degradation.

steps.prompt: The AZ recovers but targets flap. Next?

options.text: Review health-check config + recent deploys; check the canary metrics
options.why: Flapping after recovery smells like a bad deploy or misconfigured health check — evidence first.
More instances of a flapping app = more flapping. Fix the cause.

scenarios.title: Terraform Says 47 Changes
scenarios.context: Monday plan shows 47 changes nobody made. Production stack.

options.text: Review the plan resource by resource — identify console drift vs real need
options.why: The plan is the diff review: classify each change (drift to revert, drift to adopt, real change) before touching apply.
Blind apply could revert a deliberate hotfix or destroy something the drift created intentionally.
Deleting state orphans real resources — the nuclear option for a reading problem.

steps.prompt: 40 changes are console drift (someone scaled manually), 7 are your intended updates. Move?

options.text: Import/adopt the intentional drift into config, revert the rest via targeted apply, document the rule
options.why: Adopt what's deliberate (write it into config), revert the rest, and set the team rule: infra changes go through Terraform.
Applies the 7 you want and reverts 40 someone may depend on — without telling anyone.

Multi-AZ everywhere · decouple with SQS · SG stateful / NACL stateless · Aurora=relational, DynamoDB=key-value · Savings Plans for baseline
PIM kills standing admin · Policy governs config, RBAC governs access · Zones > sets · Private Endpoints for PaaS · hub-spoke, non-transitive peering
SCPs bound, IAM grants · ABAC via tags · org Trail + Object Lock · KMS envelope encryption · WAF rate rules for floods
Git is truth, cluster is cache · Argo CD syncs · drift detected not debated · Rollouts for progressive delivery

answerBank.a: By job market target: AWS for startups/scale-ups breadth, Azure for enterprise/Microsoft shops. The concepts transfer ~80% (IAM/RBAC, VPC/VNet, S3/Blob). Pick one, go deep, then map the second in weeks not months.

CKA if you'll operate clusters; CKAD if you'll ship apps to them. Most learners benefit from CKA first — the admin mental model makes the developer exam easier. Both are performance-based: practice in live clusters.

Terraform for multi-cloud and marketability; CloudFormation/ARM for deep single-cloud shops. Learn Terraform first (the concepts transfer), then read the native tool. This module's Associate prep is Terraform.

answerBank.q: How do I practice CKS without a budget?
answerBank.a: Local clusters (kind/k3d) + Falco + a vulnerability scanner. The CKS skills (hardening, supply chain, runtime) all run locally. The exam environment is remote but the skills are identical.

answerBank.q: Zero trust — where do I actually start?
answerBank.a: Identity: phishing-resistant MFA everywhere + PIM for admins. That's 60% of the value. Then device posture, then microsegmentation. The module sequences SP 800-207 into this order.

Vault for multi-cloud/dynamic secrets/PKI-as-a-service; cloud-native secrets managers for single-cloud simplicity. Learn Vault's model (engines/auth/policies) — it teaches secrets thinking that transfers.
